Here are one user's logins over the first thirteen days of January. Four days have no login, and the other nine fall into three streaks. Which days are missing? How long is each streak? Which login is the latest? Questions like these fill the sequel round of a data engineering interview. This video answers twenty-two of them. Eleven get worked through on real queries in DuckDB. The other eleven come quickly, at the end. Most of them start by numbering rows.

Question one. What's the difference between rank, dense rank, and row number? Here are the page's twenty-four players, ordered by score. Four of them tie at eighty. Row number gives each row its own number, so the tie is broken arbitrarily. Rank lets them share thirteen, then skips to seventeen. Dense rank shares ten, then goes on to eleven, with no gap. Question two. How do you keep only the latest row per key? Number each user's events from the newest, and keep number one. Twenty-four events go in, and ten rows come out: one per user. Use row number, not rank. Give user three two events at the same moment, and rank numbers both of them one, so user three comes back twice. Row number keeps exactly one, though which one is arbitrary without a tiebreaker. Question three. What is qualify, and which engines support it? It filters on a window function after it's computed, the way having filters an aggregate. The subquery goes, and the same ten rows come back. DuckDB, BigQuery, Snowflake and Databricks support it. Postgres and my sequel don't, so there you keep the subquery. So why can't that filter just go in WHERE? Because of the order a query runs in.
